slides.title: Why do we ask "why"?
slides.text: Asking why helps you learn new things. Ice melts because the sun is warm. Try asking “why?” about one thing you notice today.

slides.title: It's okay to ask questions
slides.text: It is okay to ask a question when you feel confused. Good thinkers ask lots of questions. If something does not make sense, asking is one way to learn.

slides.title: Look closely first
slides.text: A bug on the ground might look scary at first. Look closely before you decide — it might just be a tiny ladybug. First look, then decide.

slides.title: Same or different?
slides.text: Look closely at two toys to compare them. A ball is round, but a block is square. Comparing helps your brain notice important details.

slides.title: Real or pretend?
slides.text: A cartoon dragon that breathes fire is pretend. A real dog barking next to you is real. Ask yourself, “Could this really happen?”

slides.title: Looking for clues
slides.text: Clues can help you solve a mystery. Wet shoes might mean that it rained outside. A clue is a small piece of information that helps you figure something out.

slides.title: Two clues together
slides.text: One clue helps you guess. Two matching clues help even more. Muddy paw prints and a wagging tail both mean your dog was outside. More matching clues can make your idea stronger.

slides.title: Listening all the way
slides.text: Listen to the whole story before you decide what happened. The middle of a story can change everything. Hear the whole story before making up your mind.

slides.title: Checking with a grown-up
slides.text: You are not sure if something is true. Ask a grown-up you trust to help. When you are unsure, checking with someone trustworthy can help.

slides.title: Guess or really know?
slides.text: A guess is what you think might be true. Checking gives you more information. If you think there are 8 blocks, count them to see whether your guess was right. Guess first if you need to, then check.

quiz.question: Why do we ask "why"?
choices: To learn new things
For no reason at all
quiz.explanation: When you ask “why?”, your brain looks for a reason., like asking why leaves change color in fall.

quiz.question: Is it okay to ask a question when something feels confusing?
choices: Yes, that's smart
No, never ask questions
quiz.explanation: Yes! Asking questions helps you learn, like asking why the sky is blue. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: You see a bug on the ground. What should you do before deciding it's scary?
choices: Look closely at it first
Assume it's scary right away
quiz.explanation: Looking carefully gives you more information before you decide. what's really there. A scary bug might just be a friendly ladybug.

quiz.question: A ball and a block — are they the same shape?
choices: No, one is round and one is square
Yes, they are exactly the same
quiz.explanation: Looking closely shows how things differ. A ball is round, but a block is square. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: A cartoon dragon that breathes fire — is that real or pretend?
choices: Pretend
Real
quiz.explanation: Cartoons show pretend things, like a fire-breathing dragon. Your barking dog is really there. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: Your shoes are wet. What clue could explain why?
choices: It rained outside
Shoes always get wet for no reason
quiz.explanation: A clue is a little piece of information that helps you solve the question. what happened. Wet shoes can mean it rained outside.

quiz.question: Muddy paw prints and a wagging tail both hint your dog was outside. Do two matching clues help more than just one?
choices: Yes, two matching clues help more
No, one clue is just as good as two
quiz.explanation: Two matching clues make you more sure than just one. Muddy paws and a wagging tail both say your dog went outside.

quiz.question: Your friend starts telling you a story. Should you listen to the whole thing before deciding what happened?
choices: Yes, listen all the way through
No, guess after just the first word
quiz.explanation: Hearing the whole story gives you more information before you decide. helps you understand it. The middle can change everything.

quiz.question: You hear something surprising. What should you do?
choices: Ask a grown-up you trust
Just believe it right away
quiz.explanation: A trusted grown-up can help you know what's true. They can check a surprising story for you. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: A guess might be wrong. What helps you know for sure?
choices: Looking closely to check
Never checking at all
quiz.explanation: Looking closely turns a guess into something you really know. Counting your blocks again shows the true number.

slides.title: Think before you act
slides.text: Before you act, give your brain a tiny pause. Ask, “What could happen next?” For example, before grabbing a toy from someone, you can think of a kinder choice, like asking for a turn.

slides.title: Slow down to be sure
slides.text: You count your blocks fast and aren't sure of the number. Counting again slowly helps you know for sure. Going a little slower can help you catch mistakes.

slides.title: Sorting things into groups
slides.text: Put your toys into matching groups. All the cars go together, and all the animals go together. Grouping similar things makes patterns easier to see.

slides.title: Which is more?
slides.text: One plate has 3 cookies. Another plate has 5 cookies. Counting them tells you which plate has more. Count or compare instead of guessing.

slides.title: What comes next?
slides.text: Look at this pattern: red, blue, red, blue. Can you guess what color comes next? Patterns help you predict what may come next.

slides.title: Guessing what happens next
slides.text: The sky fills up with big dark clouds. That is a clue that rain might be coming soon. Use clues to make a smart prediction, but remember a prediction can still be wrong.

slides.title: What made it happen?
slides.text: Things happen for a reason, and we can look for the cause. If a plant gets water and sunlight, those things help it grow. Asking “what made this happen?” helps you understand cause and effect. Ask, “What happened first, and what happened because of it?”

slides.title: Changing your mind
slides.text: You can change your mind when you learn something new. That does not mean you did something wrong — it means your brain used new information to make a better choice. New information can help you make a better decision.

slides.title: Picking the best choice
slides.text: When you have choices, compare what each one gives you. An apple and candy can both taste good, but an apple usually keeps you full longer. Thinking about what you need helps you choose. Think about what you want now and what will help you later.

slides.title: Try it again if it doesn't work
slides.text: A puzzle piece does not fit in the spot. Try a different piece instead of giving up. If one idea fails, change something and try again.

quiz.question: What should you do before you act?
choices: Stop and think first
Just do it right away
quiz.explanation: Stopping to think first helps you choose well, like looking both ways before you cross the street. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: You count your blocks fast and aren't sure you got it right. What should you do?
choices: Count again slowly to be sure
Just guess and move on
quiz.explanation: Checking your work can catch a mistake. helps you get the right number. Guessing fast can be wrong.

quiz.question: What is a good way to organize your toys?
choices: Put them into matching groups
Mix them all together
quiz.explanation: Sorting into groups, like putting all your cars together, makes your toys easier to find. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: One plate has 3 cookies, another has 5. Which plate has more?
choices: The plate with 5
They both have the same amount
quiz.explanation: Counting carefully tells you which is more. Five cookies is more than three. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: Red, blue, red, blue, red... what comes next?
choices: Blue
Green
quiz.explanation: A pattern is something that repeats in a predictable way.. After red comes blue, then red again. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: The sky fills up with big dark clouds. What might that mean?
choices: It might rain soon
The clouds mean nothing at all
quiz.explanation: Big dark clouds are a clue. They can mean rain is coming soon. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: A plant grows tall because you gave it water every day. What made it grow?
choices: Watering it
Nothing made it happen
quiz.explanation: Watering the plant is the cause. It growing tall is the effect. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: You learn something new that shows you were wrong. What should you do?
choices: Change your mind
Never change your mind
quiz.explanation: Learning something new can show your first idea was wrong. Changing your mind then is okay. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: An apple and a piece of candy are both snack choices. Which one keeps you full longer?
choices: The apple
They are exactly the same
quiz.explanation: An apple keeps your tummy full longer than candy. It has more of what your body needs. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

quiz.question: A puzzle piece does not fit where you tried it. What should you do?
choices: Try a different piece
Give up right away
quiz.explanation: Trying a different piece, instead of giving up, helps you solve the puzzle. That is a smart way to check instead of only guessing.

slides.title: Fact vs. opinion
slides.text: A fact is something true that you can check, like 'the sun is hot.' An opinion is what someone feels or believes, like 'summer is the best season.' A useful habit is to ask: “Can I check this, or is it someone’s view?”

slides.title: Asking good questions
slides.text: Good thinkers ask follow-up questions instead of just accepting an answer, like 'how do you know that?' If a friend says a game is the best ever, ask what makes it the best. Questions such as “How do you know?” and “What evidence do you have?” help you dig deeper.

slides.title: More than one answer
slides.text: Some questions have more than one good answer, so it pays to think of a few options. Picking between reading, playing outside, or building something often leads to a better choice. Before choosing, try thinking of at least two possibilities.

slides.title: Spotting an exaggeration
slides.text: Some statements sound like facts but are really big opinions in disguise. "This is the best pizza in the entire universe" can't actually be checked or proven — it just sounds confident. Words like “always,” “never,” and “best ever” are clues to check the claim carefully.

slides.title: Don't believe everything right away
slides.text: Something isn't automatically true just because it's written down or posted online. A video claiming a trick will make you "super strong instantly" should make you pause and wonder. Pause before you believe, share, or act on surprising information.

slides.title: A picture doesn't tell the whole story
slides.text: A photo only shows one moment, chosen by whoever took it. A picture of a messy room might have been taken right after a fun project, not because someone is messy all the time. Ask what happened before and after the picture was taken.

slides.title: Checking with a trusted source
slides.text: When you're not sure if something is true, ask a grown-up or check a trusted book. If a friend says elephants can't jump, a nature book can tell you if that's really true. Good sources help you check a claim instead of just repeating it.

slides.title: Checking more than one place
slides.text: If something you read seems surprising, check whether another trusted source says the same thing. When two or three good sources agree, you can trust the information more. Independent sources that agree can give you more confidence.

slides.title: Why is someone telling me this?
slides.text: People sometimes share information because it helps them, not just because it's true. An ad for a toy wants you to buy it, so it will only mention the good parts. Ask what the speaker wants you to think, feel, buy, or do.

slides.title: It's okay to disagree
slides.text: Two people can look at the same thing and see it differently, and that's normal. You might think a book's ending was happy while your friend thinks it was sad, and you can both still be great friends. You can challenge an idea without attacking the person.

quiz.question: "The movie is 90 minutes long" vs "the movie was boring" — which is the fact?
choices: "The movie is 90 minutes long," since it can be checked
"The movie was boring," since it can be checked
quiz.explanation: A fact can be checked, like timing a movie to see it really is 90 minutes long. An opinion, like "it was boring," just depends on how you feel.

quiz.question: What is an "opinion"?
choices: What someone thinks or feels
Something that can be proven true or false
quiz.explanation: An opinion is what someone personally thinks or feels, not something everyone must agree on. Your friend might love broccoli while you think it's terrible.

quiz.question: A friend says "this game is the best one ever." What's a smart follow-up question?
choices: "What makes it the best?"
Believe it immediately with no questions
quiz.explanation: Asking "what makes it the best?" pushes past a big claim to find the real reasons behind it. Good thinkers dig deeper instead of just nodding along.

quiz.question: You want to spend your free time well — reading, playing outside, or building something. Is there only one right choice?
choices: No, several choices could be good ones
Yes, there's always exactly one right answer
quiz.explanation: Several activities, like reading or building, can all be good choices for your time. Comparing a few options usually leads to a better pick than grabbing the first idea.

quiz.question: "This is the best pizza in the entire universe!" — is that a checkable fact or an opinion dressed up big?
choices: An opinion, even though it sounds like a fact
A fact anyone could prove
quiz.explanation: Saying something is "the best in the entire universe" sounds bold, but nobody could actually check every pizza everywhere. Confident words don't automatically make a statement a fact.

quiz.question: Does everything you read online automatically become true?
choices: No, it should be checked
Yes, if it's written down it's always true
quiz.explanation: Anyone can post anything online, true or not, so posting alone doesn't prove it. A video claiming a trick makes you "instantly super strong" should make you pause and check.

quiz.question: A friend says elephants can't jump. How can you find out if that's really true?
choices: Check a trusted book or ask an adult
Just believe your friend, no need to check
quiz.explanation: Trusted sources, like a nature book or a knowledgeable adult, can confirm whether a claim is really true. Checking beats just trusting a friend's guess. The key is to check where the information came from and whether the evidence really supports it.

quiz.question: You read a surprising claim in one place. What's a smart next step?
choices: Check if another trusted source says the same thing
Believe it because you read it once
quiz.explanation: When two or three trusted sources agree on the same surprising claim, you can trust it much more. One single source could simply be mistaken. The key is to check where the information came from and whether the evidence really supports it.

quiz.question: An ad for a toy only mentions the good parts. Why?
choices: Because the ad wants you to buy the toy
Ads always tell the full, balanced truth
quiz.explanation: Ads want you to buy the toy, so they show only the fun parts and skip the annoying ones. Asking why someone is telling you something helps you judge it fairly.

quiz.question: Does disagreeing with a friend mean the friendship is in trouble?
choices: No, respectful disagreement is normal
Yes, friends must always agree on everything
quiz.explanation: Two people can watch the same movie and honestly feel differently about the ending. Respectful disagreement, like that, doesn't have to hurt a friendship at all.

slides.title: Cause and effect
slides.text: A cause is why something happened, and an effect is what happened because of it. Forgetting to water a plant is the cause, and the plant wilting days later is the effect. Look for evidence that the cause actually helped produce the effect.

slides.title: Being a detective
slides.text: A good detective checks several clues before deciding what happened, instead of guessing from just one. If a plant is dying, check its sunlight, water, and soil before assuming you know why. Check several clues and consider more than one explanation.

slides.title: Spotting assumptions
slides.text: An assumption is something you believe without checking if it's true. Saying 'he must be fast because he's tall' assumes something about him that might not be true at all. An assumption is a hidden “maybe” that is being treated like a fact.

slides.title: Correlation isn't causation
slides.text: Two things happening at the same time doesn't mean one caused the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both go up in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn. When two things move together, ask whether a third factor could explain both.

slides.title: One example isn't proof
slides.text: One example doesn't prove something is always true, even if it seems convincing. Just because one dog you met was friendly doesn't mean every dog you'll ever meet will be friendly too. One example can start a question, but it usually cannot settle the whole question.

slides.title: Big claims need big evidence
slides.text: A huge claim, like "this vitamin cures every sickness," needs strong proof behind it. One person's story isn't enough evidence for a claim that big. The stronger or more surprising the claim, the stronger the evidence should be.

slides.title: Following the thread
slides.text: If a friend says "cats hate water," a good next question is "how do you know?" Asking that a few times in a row often leads back to real evidence, or shows there wasn't much to begin with. Keep asking where a claim came from until you reach evidence you can evaluate.

slides.title: Guessing then testing
slides.text: You guess a plant isn't growing well because it needs more light. Moving it to a sunnier spot and watching what happens next actually tests your guess instead of just hoping you're right. A test helps separate a good guess from a true explanation.

slides.title: Small numbers can trick you
slides.text: Flipping a coin three times and getting heads every time doesn't mean the coin will always land on heads. A few tries can look like a pattern even when it's really just luck. A bigger sample usually gives you a more reliable picture.

slides.title: Changing your mind
slides.text: A good thinker isn't afraid to change their mind when new information shows their first idea was wrong. Learning an animal is actually a mammal, not a reptile, is a reason to update your belief. New information can help you make a better decision.

quiz.question: You forgot to water a plant, and a few days later it wilted. What does "cause and effect" mean here?
choices: Understanding that forgetting to water it (cause) led to it wilting (effect)
A game with no real meaning
quiz.explanation: A cause is why something happens, and an effect is what happens as a result. Forgetting to water the plant caused it to wilt days later. A good thinker asks whether there is another explanation before deciding what caused what.

quiz.question: A plant is dying. What does a good detective-thinker do before deciding why?
choices: Checks several clues, like sunlight, water, and soil
Guesses after just one clue
quiz.explanation: Good detectives look at several clues, like sunlight, water, and soil, before deciding what's wrong. Guessing from just one clue can lead to a wrong answer.

quiz.question: Saying "he must be fast because he's tall" — what is that an example of?
choices: An assumption — believing something without checking
A proven fact
quiz.explanation: An assumption is a belief you haven't actually checked, like guessing someone is fast just because they're tall. Height doesn't actually tell you anything about someone's speed. A good thinker notices the assumption and asks what evidence would actually confirm it.

quiz.question: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
choices: No, they just happen at the same time
Yes, anything that happens together must be connected
quiz.explanation: Ice cream and sunburns both happen more in summer because of the hot weather, not because one causes the other. Two things rising together doesn't mean either one caused the other. A good thinker asks whether there is another explanation before deciding what caused what.

quiz.question: One dog you met was friendly. Does that prove every dog you'll ever meet will be friendly too?
choices: No, one example isn't proof
Yes, one example proves it for all dogs
quiz.explanation: Meeting one friendly dog only tells you about that single dog, not every dog everywhere. It takes many examples, not just one, to prove something is usually true.

quiz.question: "This vitamin cures every sickness" is a huge claim. What does a claim that big need?
choices: Strong evidence, not just one story
No evidence at all, since it sounds nice
quiz.explanation: A claim that huge, like curing every sickness, needs lots of strong proof, not just one person's story. Bigger claims generally need stronger evidence to back them up. The key is to check where the information came from and whether the evidence really supports it.

quiz.question: A friend says "cats hate water." What's a good way to check if that's really true?
choices: Keep asking "how do you know?" until you reach real evidence
Repeat it to others without checking
quiz.explanation: Asking "how do you know?" a few times often leads back to real evidence, or shows there wasn't much to begin with. It's a simple way to test a claim before repeating it. The key is to check where the information came from and whether the evidence really supports it.

quiz.question: You guess a plant isn't growing because it needs more light. What should you do next?
choices: Move it to more light and see what happens
Just assume your guess is correct
quiz.explanation: Moving the plant to more light and watching what happens actually tests your guess instead of just hoping. That's how you find out if an idea is really true.

quiz.question: You flip a coin 3 times and get heads all 3 times. Does that mean the coin always lands heads?
choices: No, that could just be luck with a few flips
Yes, 3 flips proves it always lands heads
quiz.explanation: Three flips is too few to prove a pattern — it's easy to get heads three times just by luck. Flipping many more times would show what the coin really does.

quiz.question: Is it okay to change your mind if you learn new information?
choices: Yes, that's what good thinkers do
No, you should never change your mind
quiz.explanation: Good thinkers update their ideas when new evidence shows the old idea was wrong. Learning a "lizard" is actually a salamander is a good reason to change your mind.

slides.title: Evaluating evidence
slides.text: Before believing a claim, it helps to ask: what evidence supports it? Is the evidence strong, weak, or missing entirely? For example, if a classmate claims "this energy drink makes you smarter," asking what actual studies or evidence back that up — versus just a company's advertisement — helps you judge whether it's really true. The thinking move: Ask what the evidence is, how it was collected, and whether it actually supports the claim.

slides.title: What makes evidence strong?
slides.text: Not all evidence is equally solid — a claim backed by one blog post is much weaker than one backed by ten independent studies that all found the same thing. Before trusting a claim, it's worth asking how much real evidence actually stands behind it, and how independent that evidence is. The thinking move: Strong evidence is relevant, repeatable, and supported by more than one independent source.

slides.title: Checking the source
slides.text: Who is saying this, and why? A source with something to gain from you believing a claim deserves a closer, more careful look. For example, an ad for a supplement claiming it "boosts brainpower" comes from a company that profits if you believe it — which is exactly why it deserves more scrutiny than a neutral science article on the same topic. The thinking move: A source can still be useful even if it has an interest, but that interest is a reason to check more carefully.

slides.title: Correlation isn't causation
slides.text: Just because two things happen around the same time doesn't mean one caused the other. Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer — but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn. For example, if students who play a certain video game also tend to get good grades, that doesn't necessarily mean the game caused the good grades — maybe both are just linked to having more free time at home. The thinking move: When two things move together, ask whether a third factor could explain both.

slides.title: Cherry-picking data
slides.text: Cherry-picking means showing only the evidence that supports your point while quietly leaving out the evidence that doesn't. For example, a company's report might highlight the one month sales went up while leaving out the five months they went down, creating a misleading picture from real, but incomplete, numbers. The thinking move: Always ask what information might have been left out.

slides.title: Percent vs. actual numbers
slides.text: A headline like "cases tripled!" sounds alarming, but tripling from 1 case to 3 cases in a school of 2,000 students is barely anything at all. Checking the actual numbers behind a percentage often changes how alarming — or unalarming — a claim really is. The thinking move: Check both the percentage and the starting number before deciding how big a change really is.

slides.title: Averages can mislead
slides.text: An average can hide a lot — a class 'average score' of 75% might mean everyone scored near 75%, or it might mean half scored 100% and half scored 50%. For example, two classes could both report a 75% average test score, but one class might have every student scoring close to 75%, while the other has half the class acing it and half failing badly — very different situations hidden behind the same number. The thinking move: An average is useful, but the spread of the numbers matters too.

slides.title: One story isn't the whole story
slides.text: A single dramatic story can feel more convincing than a pile of boring statistics, even when the statistics tell the broader picture. For example, hearing one scary story about a plane crash can make flying feel dangerous, even though the actual data shows that flying is one of the safest ways to travel. The thinking move: Personal stories can be powerful, but broader data helps show what is typical.

slides.title: Can it be repeated?
slides.text: If an experiment finds a surprising result once, but nobody else can get the same result when they try it again, that's a warning sign the original finding might not be real. Results that hold up when other people repeat the test are far more trustworthy than a one-time surprise. The thinking move: Results become more convincing when independent people can reproduce them.

quiz.question: A classmate claims "this energy drink makes you smarter." What should you check first?
choices: What evidence actually supports it
Nothing — just believe confident-sounding claims
quiz.explanation: Before believing a bold claim, ask what real evidence backs it up, like actual studies rather than just an advertisement. A company's ad for its own energy drink isn't neutral proof — it's trying to sell you something.

quiz.question: A claim backed by one blog post vs. backed by ten independent scientific studies — which is stronger evidence?
choices: Ten independent studies
They're equally strong
quiz.explanation: Ten independent studies that all reach the same conclusion are far stronger evidence than a single blog post written by one person. When many separate sources agree, it's much less likely they're all wrong by coincidence. This habit helps you separate a convincing-sounding claim from one that is actually well supported.

quiz.question: An ad for a "brain-boosting" supplement comes from the company selling it. Why does that matter?
choices: A source with something to gain deserves closer scrutiny
The source of a claim never matters
quiz.explanation: A source that profits from you believing something, like a company selling its own supplement, has a reason to shade the truth in its favor. That does not necessarily mean it's lying, but it does mean the claim deserves extra scrutiny.

quiz.question: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
choices: No — correlation isn't the same as causation
Yes, if two things happen together one always causes the other
quiz.explanation: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer because hot weather causes both, not because one causes the other. Mixing up correlation with causation is a common thinking mistake worth watching for. This habit helps you separate a convincing-sounding claim from one that is actually well supported.

quiz.question: A company's report shows only the one month sales went up, hiding the five months they went down. What's this called?
choices: Cherry-picking data
A completely fair, balanced report
quiz.explanation: Cherry-picking means showing only the evidence that supports your point, like a company's report bragging about one good sales month while quietly hiding five bad ones. The numbers shown are real, but the picture they create is misleading.

quiz.question: A school goes from 1 case of a cold to 3 cases out of 2,000 students, and a headline says "cases tripled!" What's misleading about that?
choices: The percentage sounds scary but the actual numbers are tiny
Nothing — tripling is always a huge, alarming deal
quiz.explanation: A percentage like "tripled" can sound alarming while describing a tiny, real number — going from 1 case to 3 out of 2,000 students barely changes anything. Checking the actual numbers behind a scary-sounding percentage often reveals it's not a big deal.

quiz.question: Two classes both average 75% on a test, but one has scores clustered near 75% while the other is half 100s and half 50s. What does this show?
choices: Yes, very different sets of numbers can share the same average
No, an average always tells the whole story
quiz.explanation: An average can hide very different realities behind the same number — one class scoring evenly near 75%, another split between students acing it and students failing it, can report an identical average. That's why it's worth asking what's behind an average, not just trusting the number.

quiz.question: A dramatic story about a plane crash can make flying feel dangerous, even though data shows flying is very safe. Why?
choices: A vivid story can feel more convincing than statistics, even when it's misleading
Stories are always more accurate than data
quiz.explanation: One dramatic story, like a plane crash, can feel far more convincing than a page of statistics, even when the statistics tell the broader statistical picture. Flying remains one of the safest ways to travel, despite how scary a single vivid story can feel.

quiz.question: An experiment gets a surprising result, but no one else can repeat it. What should that make you think?
choices: Be cautious — it might not be a real, reliable effect
Trust it completely since it happened once
quiz.explanation: If nobody else can get the same result when they repeat an experiment, that's a warning sign the original finding might have been a fluke, not a real effect. Trustworthy results tend to hold up when other people test them independently.

quiz.question: Is "lots of people believe it" the same thing as strong evidence?
choices: No, popularity isn't proof
Yes, if enough people believe something it must be true
quiz.explanation: How many people believe something does not by itself prove that it is true — plenty of popular beliefs throughout history turned out to be completely wrong. Real evidence comes from checking facts, not counting votes. This habit helps you separate a convincing-sounding claim from one that is actually well supported.

slides.title: Spotting assumptions
slides.text: An assumption is something believed without proof. Noticing hidden assumptions in an argument helps you judge whether it actually holds up. For example, the argument "he must be good at math because he's Asian" hides an unproven assumption about a whole group of people, which makes the argument weak the moment you notice it. The thinking move: An assumption is a hidden “maybe” that is being treated like a fact.

slides.title: Stereotypes vs. individuals
slides.text: A stereotype is a generalization applied to a whole group, and it says nothing reliable about any one specific person in that group. Assuming a new classmate is bad at sports because of where they're from tells you nothing real about that individual kid. The thinking move: Group patterns should never be treated as a shortcut for judging an individual person.

slides.title: Considering other perspectives
slides.text: Understanding how a situation looks from someone else's point of view often reveals things your own perspective alone would miss. For example, a disagreement between two group project members might look totally different once you understand that one person was juggling other responsibilities the other didn't know about. The thinking move: A different point of view can reveal facts or priorities you missed.

slides.title: Everyone has a blind spot
slides.text: Your own experiences quietly shape what problems feel obvious to you and which ones you barely notice. Someone who's never dealt with money trouble might assume budgeting is "just common sense," without realizing how hard it actually is for someone juggling unpredictable bills. The thinking move: Ask what your own experience might be causing you to overlook.

slides.title: Weighing both sides
slides.text: On a genuinely debatable topic, looking fairly at the strongest arguments on both sides — before forming an opinion — leads to more solid conclusions. For example, before deciding your opinion on whether school should start later, actually reading the strongest arguments on both sides — about sleep and about schedules — leads to a more solid opinion than just picking a side because it sounds nice. The thinking move: Compare the strongest evidence and reasoning on each side, not just the easiest arguments to attack.

slides.title: Groupthink
slides.text: Groupthink happens when a group moves toward agreement so quickly that individual doubts never get voiced out loud. A class might loudly agree a plan is great, even though privately, several students have real concerns they never mention. The thinking move: A group can sound confident even when important doubts have not been voiced.

slides.title: Thinking for yourself in a group
slides.text: When everyone around you agrees quickly, it can feel easier to go along with the group than to raise a doubt out loud. For example, if a group project is rushing toward a plan you think has a flaw, speaking up — even briefly — gives the group a chance to catch a mistake before it becomes a real problem. The thinking move: Independent thinking means being willing to ask a respectful question when everyone else agrees.

slides.title: Updating your view
slides.text: Being able to say "I was wrong" and change your mind when solid new evidence appears is a strength, not a failure. For example, if you were sure a friend forgot your birthday on purpose, but then learned their phone had been broken all week, updating your opinion based on that new fact is exactly what a careful thinker does. The thinking move: Changing your conclusion when the evidence changes is a sign of careful thinking.

slides.title: Being wrong doesn't make you dumb
slides.text: A scientist whose theory gets disproven by better evidence isn't a failure — that's exactly how scientific progress works. Treating being wrong as a normal, expected part of learning makes it much easier to update your views instead of defending them out of pride. The thinking move: Mistakes become useful when you use them to improve your model of the world.

quiz.question: What is an "assumption"?
choices: Something believed without proof
A fact that has been proven true
quiz.explanation: An assumption is something you believe without actually checking whether it's true, and it can quietly weaken an argument built on top of it. Noticing the assumption hiding inside a claim is the first step to testing whether the claim really holds up.

quiz.question: Assuming a new classmate is bad at sports because of where they're from — is that fair reasoning?
choices: No, a group generalization says nothing about one specific person
Yes, group generalizations always apply to individuals
quiz.explanation: Assuming a classmate is bad at sports because of where they're from is a stereotype, a guess about a whole group applied to one specific person. It tells you nothing real about that individual kid, who might actually be a great athlete.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to consider other people's perspectives?
choices: It can reveal things your own viewpoint alone would miss
Other perspectives are never worth considering
quiz.explanation: Seeing a situation from someone else's point of view can reveal details your own perspective completely misses, like realizing a distracted teammate was actually dealing with a problem at home. Considering other perspectives leads to fairer, more accurate judgments.

quiz.question: Someone who's never struggled with money might assume budgeting is 'just common sense.' What does this show?
choices: Your own background can create a blind spot to others' struggles
Everyone experiences every situation in exactly the same way
quiz.explanation: Your own experiences quietly shape what feels obvious to you and what you barely notice in someone else's life. Someone who's never struggled financially might assume budgeting is simple, not realizing how hard it is when bills are unpredictable.

quiz.question: Before forming an opinion on a genuinely debatable topic like school start times, what should you do?
choices: Look fairly at the strongest arguments on both sides
Only read arguments that already match your opinion
quiz.explanation: On a genuinely debatable topic, like whether school should start later, reading the strongest arguments on both sides — about sleep and about schedules — before deciding leads to a more solid opinion. Picking a side just because it sounds nice skips this important step.

quiz.question: A class loudly agrees a plan is great, even though many privately have doubts. What's this called?
choices: Groupthink — going along with the crowd
Careful, independent thinking
quiz.explanation: Groupthink happens when a group rushes to agree so quickly that individual doubts never get said out loud, even though several people privately disagree. A class might loudly praise a plan while many students secretly have real concerns.

quiz.question: A group is rushing toward a plan you think has a flaw. What does independent thinking suggest doing?
choices: Speaking up, even if it feels uncomfortable
Staying quiet so you don't disrupt the group
quiz.explanation: When everyone around you agrees fast, it feels easier to stay quiet than to raise a doubt, even a small one. Speaking up anyway, even briefly, gives the group a real chance to catch a mistake before it becomes a bigger problem.

quiz.question: You were sure a friend forgot your birthday on purpose, but learn their phone was broken all week. What should you do?
choices: Update your belief based on the new information
Keep believing the original idea no matter what
quiz.explanation: Updating your belief once you learn new facts, like discovering your friend's phone was broken all week, is exactly what a careful thinker does. Sticking with your first assumption after learning it was wrong means ignoring information that matters.

quiz.question: A scientist's theory gets disproven by better evidence. Does that make the scientist a failure?
choices: No, updating theories with better evidence is how progress happens
Yes, a disproven theory always means failure
quiz.explanation: A scientist whose theory gets disproven by better evidence is not automatically a failure; revising ideas is part of science, since updating ideas based on evidence is how knowledge actually improves. Treating being wrong as normal makes it much easier to keep learning.

quiz.question: Saying "she must not like sports because she wears glasses" — what is that?
choices: An unproven assumption
A proven fact
quiz.explanation: This statement links wearing glasses to disliking sports with zero actual evidence connecting the two things, which makes it an unproven assumption rather than a fact. Noticing this kind of gap is exactly how you catch weak reasoning.

slides.title: Defining the real problem
slides.text: Sometimes what looks like the problem is actually just a symptom of a different, deeper problem. Defining the real issue is the first step to solving it well. For example, a student who keeps falling asleep in class might seem lazy, but the real problem could be staying up too late — fixing bedtime, not "trying harder to stay awake," is what actually solves it. The thinking move: A clear problem statement prevents you from solving the wrong thing.

slides.title: Root cause vs. quick fix
slides.text: A bike chain that keeps falling off can be oiled again and again, but if the chain itself is stretched out, oiling it is only ever a quick fix. Finding the actual root cause — replacing the stretched chain — solves the problem instead of just delaying it. The thinking move: A quick fix treats the symptom; a root-cause solution addresses what keeps creating the problem.

slides.title: Breaking a big problem into parts
slides.text: A goal like "get better at math" is so big and vague that it's hard to know where to even start. Breaking it into something specific, like "practice fractions for fifteen minutes a day," turns an overwhelming goal into something you can actually do. The thinking move: Smaller, specific steps make progress easier to start and measure.

slides.title: Setting a goal and checking progress
slides.text: Deciding what you're aiming for, then regularly checking whether your approach is actually getting you closer, keeps effort from being wasted. For example, if your goal is to improve a test score, checking after a few practice tests whether your study method is actually helping lets you switch strategies early instead of wasting weeks on something that isn't working. The thinking move: A goal is more useful when you can tell whether your strategy is working.

slides.title: Testing your solution
slides.text: After trying a new study method, checking whether your next quiz score actually improved tells you if it really worked — assuming it helped just because it felt different isn't the same as knowing. The thinking move: Decide what result would count as improvement before you test the solution.

slides.title: Working backward from the goal
slides.text: Planning a big project by starting at the deadline and figuring out what needs to happen each week before it often works better than just starting at the beginning and hoping. Working backward from the goal turns a vague deadline into a clear weekly plan. The thinking move: Start with the outcome, then identify the steps and deadlines needed to reach it.

slides.title: Asking better questions
slides.text: The quality of your thinking often depends on the quality of your questions — a vague question gets a vague answer. For example, instead of asking "is this a good school?" asking "good at what, and good for whom?" forces a much more specific, useful answer than the original question ever could. The thinking move: Precise questions usually produce more useful answers.

slides.title: Ruling out the obvious wrong answer
slides.text: On a hard multiple-choice question, eliminating the choices you already know are wrong first makes the remaining decision much easier. Ruling out bad options is often a faster path to the right one than staring at all of them at once. The thinking move: Eliminating clearly wrong options reduces the problem you still need to solve.

slides.title: When to ask for help
slides.text: Being stuck on one problem for thirty minutes without progress is usually a sign that it's a good time to ask for help, not a sign of failure. Knowing when to ask is its own kind of good thinking, not a shortcut around it. The thinking move: Good problem solving includes knowing when another person, tool, or explanation could unblock you.

quiz.question: A student keeps falling asleep in class, and the real cause turns out to be a late bedtime. What does "defining the real problem" mean here?
choices: Making sure you're solving the actual issue, not just a symptom of it
Skipping straight to a solution without thinking
quiz.explanation: A student falling asleep in class might look lazy, but the real problem could be a late bedtime, something "try harder" would never fix. Defining the true underlying issue, instead of just the visible symptom, is the first step toward an actual solution.

quiz.question: A bike chain keeps falling off, and oiling it only helps for a day. What does looking for the root cause mean here?
choices: Figuring out the chain itself is stretched and needs replacing
Oiling it every single day forever without asking why
quiz.explanation: Oiling a chain that keeps falling off might help for a day, but if the chain itself is worn out, oiling is only ever a temporary patch. Replacing the stretched chain finds and fixes the actual root cause instead of repeating the same fix forever.

quiz.question: "Get better at math" is a huge, vague goal. What's a smarter way to approach it?
choices: Break it into a specific step, like practicing fractions 15 minutes a day
Just repeat the vague goal to yourself daily
quiz.explanation: A goal like "get better at math" is too big and vague to act on, so it's easy to feel stuck and never start. Breaking it into something specific and small, like practicing fractions for fifteen minutes a day, makes it something you can actually do today.

quiz.question: Why is checking progress toward a goal useful?
choices: It keeps effort from being wasted on the wrong approach
Checking progress never matters
quiz.explanation: Checking progress regularly, instead of only at the very end, catches a bad approach early before too much time is wasted on it. Testing your study method after a few practice quizzes lets you switch strategies while there's still time to improve.

quiz.question: You change your study method. How do you know if it actually helped?
choices: Check whether your next quiz score actually improved
Just assume it worked because it felt different
quiz.explanation: Checking whether your next quiz score actually went up tells you whether the new study method truly worked. Simply feeling like a method was helpful isn't the same as having real evidence that it was. This habit helps you separate a convincing-sounding claim from one that is actually well supported.

quiz.question: Planning a big project by starting at the deadline and figuring out what needs to happen each week before it — what's this approach called?
choices: Working backward from the goal
Waiting until the night before to start
quiz.explanation: Working backward from a deadline, figuring out what must happen each week before it, turns a vague due date into a clear, doable weekly plan. Starting at the beginning and just hoping things work out often leads to a last-minute scramble instead.

quiz.question: Which question is more useful: "is this a good school?" or "good at what, and for whom?"
choices: The more specific question — vague questions get vague answers
They are exactly equally useful
quiz.explanation: Vague questions tend to get vague, unhelpful answers, while specific questions force a much more useful response. Asking "good at what, and good for whom?" instead of just "is this a good school?" actually gets you information you can use.

quiz.question: On a hard multiple-choice question, what's a smart first step?
choices: Rule out the choices you know are wrong
Guess immediately without reading the choices
quiz.explanation: Eliminating answer choices you already know are wrong shrinks a hard question down to a much smaller, easier decision. This process of ruling out bad options is often faster than carefully weighing every single choice from scratch. This habit helps you separate a convincing-sounding claim from one that is actually well supported.

quiz.question: You've been stuck on one problem for 30 minutes. What does that usually mean?
choices: It's a good time to ask for help
You should never ask for help, no matter how long you're stuck
quiz.explanation: Being stuck without progress for thirty minutes is a normal, expected signal to ask for help, not proof that you've failed. Recognizing when you're stuck and knowing when to reach out is itself a valuable thinking skill. This habit helps you separate a convincing-sounding claim from one that is actually well supported.

quiz.question: A team keeps missing deadlines and everyone blames laziness, but the real issue is unclear instructions. What should the team fix first?
choices: The unclear instructions, the actual root problem
Nothing, just keep blaming laziness
quiz.explanation: Blaming laziness feels easy, but if the real cause is unclear instructions, nothing improves until that actual root problem gets fixed. Solving the wrong problem, even solving it very well, doesn't actually help the team hit its deadlines.

slides.title: What is confirmation bias?
slides.text: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice and believe information that agrees with what you already think, while ignoring information that doesn't. For example, someone convinced a certain diet is unhealthy might notice and remember every negative story about it, while barely registering the many studies showing it's fine — without even realizing they're doing it. The thinking move: A useful check is to deliberately look for credible evidence that could prove your current view wrong.

slides.title: Naming the bias helps you catch it
slides.text: Simply knowing a bias's name — like confirmation bias — makes it noticeably easier to catch it happening in your own thinking, in the moment it's happening. Psychologists have named dozens of these predictable mental shortcuts, precisely because naming them is the first step to correcting for them. The thinking move: Knowing a bias gives you a label to watch for, but noticing it still takes practice.

slides.title: Availability bias
slides.text: Availability bias is judging how common or dangerous something is by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by the real numbers. After one dramatic news story, shark attacks can feel common, even though they're extremely rare — the vivid story is simply easier to recall than the actual statistics. The thinking move: Memorable examples are not automatically common examples; base-rate data helps keep perspective.

slides.title: Negativity bias
slides.text: Negative experiences and information tend to stick in memory far more strongly than positive ones do, a pattern called negativity bias. One harsh comment among ten kind ones is often the single one still bothering you at the end of the day, even though it was a tiny fraction of what was actually said. The thinking move: Notice whether one negative event is getting more mental weight than the full set of evidence deserves.

slides.title: Self-serving bias
slides.text: Self-serving bias is the tendency to credit yourself for successes while blaming outside factors for failures. Crediting a good grade to "I'm smart" but blaming a bad grade on "the test was unfair" applies two very different standards to two outcomes that might have had the same actual cause. The thinking move: Try using the same standard when explaining your successes and your failures.

slides.title: The Dunning-Kruger idea
slides.text: People who know the least about a subject are sometimes the most overconfident about it, simply because they don't yet know enough to see what they're missing. Someone who's watched a few cooking videos can feel more confident than a line cook with years of real kitchen experience, who knows firsthand how much there still is to learn. The thinking move: Confidence and competence are different things; feedback and evidence are better guides than confidence alone.

slides.title: Anchoring bias
slides.text: Anchoring bias happens when the first number or piece of information you hear quietly shapes every judgment that comes after it, even if that first piece of information was random or irrelevant. For example, a store listing a jacket's "original price" as absurdly high right next to a "sale price" makes the sale price feel like a bargain, even if that original price was never real. The thinking move: Before accepting the first number as your reference point, ask what an independent comparison would show.

slides.title: The sunk cost fallacy
slides.text: The sunk cost fallacy is the tendency to keep investing time or money in something just because you've already invested so much, even when quitting would may no longer be the better choice. For example, finishing a boring movie "because I already sat through an hour of it" ignores the fact that the hour is gone either way, and the only real question is whether the next hour is worth it. The thinking move: Past costs cannot be recovered, so the better question is whether continuing is worth the future cost.

slides.title: Being willing to update
slides.text: Genuinely strong thinkers treat their own conclusions as open to revision — new, credible evidence should be able to change a well-reasoned mind. For example, if you strongly believed a certain study supported your view, but later learned that study was retracted for bad data, updating your opinion in light of that is a sign of strength, not weakness. The thinking move: Strong conclusions should be firm enough to use but flexible enough to change when better evidence appears.

quiz.question: Someone convinced a diet is unhealthy notices every negative story but barely registers positive studies. What is this called?
choices: Confirmation bias — favoring information that agrees with what you already believe
Always changing your opinion based on new facts
quiz.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice and remember evidence that agrees with what you already believe, while barely registering evidence that doesn't. Someone convinced a diet is unhealthy will recall every negative story vividly but skim past the many studies showing it's fine.

quiz.question: Why does it help to know the name of a bias, like 'confirmation bias'?
choices: It makes the bias easier to notice happening in your own thinking
Knowing the name has no effect on noticing it
quiz.explanation: Simply knowing a bias's name makes it noticeably easier to catch happening in your own thinking, in the actual moment it's occurring. Psychologists have named dozens of these predictable mental shortcuts precisely because naming them is the first step toward correcting for them.

quiz.question: After one scary news story, shark attacks feel common, even though they're extremely rare. What's this called?
choices: Availability bias — judging by what easily comes to mind, not real numbers
An accurate way to judge how common something is
quiz.explanation: Availability bias is judging how common or dangerous something is by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by real statistics. After one dramatic news story, shark attacks can feel common even though they're extremely rare, because the vivid story is simply easier to recall than the actual numbers.

quiz.question: One harsh comment sticks in your memory more than ten kind ones from the same day. What does this show?
choices: Negative experiences tend to stick in memory more strongly
Positive and negative experiences are always remembered equally
quiz.explanation: Negativity bias is the tendency for bad experiences to stick in memory far more strongly than good ones. One harsh comment among ten kind ones is often the single thing still bothering you at day's end, even though it was a tiny fraction of what was actually said.

quiz.question: Crediting a good grade to "I'm smart" but blaming a bad grade on "the test was unfair" — what's this?
choices: Self-serving bias
A perfectly balanced, objective view of both grades
quiz.explanation: Self-serving bias is crediting yourself for successes while blaming outside factors for failures, even when both outcomes might share the same actual cause. Saying "I'm smart" after a good grade but "the test was unfair" after a bad one applies two very different standards to two similar situations.

quiz.question: Someone who's watched a few cooking videos feels more confident than a chef with years of experience. What does this illustrate?
choices: People who know the least can be the most overconfident
More knowledge always makes people feel less confident
quiz.explanation: The Dunning-Kruger idea is that people who know the least about a subject are sometimes the most overconfident about it, simply because they don't yet know enough to see what they're missing. Someone who's watched a few cooking videos can feel more confident than a line cook with years of real experience.

quiz.question: A store lists a jacket's 'original price' as absurdly high right next to the sale price. What does this exploit?
choices: Anchoring bias — the first number shapes how later numbers feel
Nothing, the original price never affects how we judge the sale price
quiz.explanation: Anchoring bias happens when the first number you hear quietly shapes every judgment that follows, even if that first number was random or made up. A store listing a jacket's "original price" as absurdly high makes the sale price feel like a bargain, even when that original price was never real.

quiz.question: Finishing a boring movie just because you already sat through an hour of it is an example of what?
choices: The sunk cost fallacy
Steelmanning an argument
quiz.explanation: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing to invest time or money in something mainly because you've already invested so much, even when quitting is more worthwhile going forward. Finishing a boring movie "because I already sat through an hour" ignores that the hour is gone either way — the only real question is whether the next hour is worth it.

quiz.question: Should a strong thinker be willing to change a conclusion?
choices: Yes, if credible new evidence supports it
No, changing your mind is always a weakness
quiz.explanation: Strong thinkers treat their conclusions as open to revision when credible new evidence appears, rather than defending an old position out of pride. Learning that a study you relied on was retracted for bad data is exactly the kind of evidence that should change your mind.

quiz.question: A person avoids flying because of one dramatic crash story, but keeps using an app just because "I already spent so much time on it." Which two biases are at play, in order?
choices: Availability bias, then the sunk cost fallacy
Confirmation bias, then anchoring bias
quiz.explanation: Avoiding flying because of one dramatic crash story is availability bias, judging danger by how vividly an example comes to mind rather than by real statistics. Continuing to use an app just because "I already spent so much time on it" is the sunk cost fallacy, letting unrecoverable past effort steer a present choice.

slides.title: Media literacy
slides.text: Understanding who created a piece of media, why, and who it's meant to persuade helps you judge how much to trust it. For example, an article about a product's benefits written by the company that sells it deserves a different level of trust than an independent review with no financial stake in the outcome.

slides.title: Primary vs. secondary sources
slides.text: A primary source is the original material — a study itself, a direct quote, raw data. A secondary source describes or summarizes that original, like a news article about the study, and can introduce distortion, simplification, or spin along the way, even without meaning to.

slides.title: Follow the money
slides.text: Checking who funded or profits from a piece of information is a fast way to judge how much scrutiny it deserves. A "study" funded by a soda company that finds sugar isn't harmful deserves a closer, more skeptical look than an independent study with no financial stake in the result.

slides.title: Recognizing propaganda
slides.text: Propaganda uses one-sided, emotionally charged messaging to push a viewpoint rather than inform. Learning to notice it helps you separate persuasion from honest information. For example, a message using only scary language and dramatic music to push one specific opinion, while ignoring any counter-evidence entirely, is a sign you might be looking at propaganda rather than balanced information.

slides.title: Loaded language
slides.text: Loaded language uses words chosen to trigger an emotional reaction rather than to describe something neutrally. Calling a policy a "job-killing disaster" instead of "an economic change" can describe the exact same policy while pushing a reader toward a very different feeling about it.

slides.title: Clickbait headlines
slides.text: A headline like "You won't BELIEVE what happened next!" is engineered to provoke a click, not to accurately summarize what follows. Clickbait headlines often overstate, distort, or leave out the actual substance of the story underneath them.

slides.title: Weighing evidence fairly
slides.text: Strong critical thinkers weigh the quality and quantity of evidence on all sides before forming a conclusion — not just picking whichever side feels more comfortable. For example, when researching a controversial topic for a school paper, deliberately reading strong arguments on both sides, not just the ones that confirm what you already believed, produces a far more credible paper.

slides.title: Burden of proof
slides.text: The burden of proof is the idea that whoever makes a claim is responsible for backing it up — not the other way around. For example, if someone claims a supplement cures headaches, it's their job to show real evidence for that, not everyone else's job to prove that it doesn't.

slides.title: Separating feelings from facts
slides.text: Recognizing when a strong emotional reaction — anger, excitement, fear — might be clouding a decision helps you think more clearly under pressure. For example, feeling furious after reading one upsetting headline might push you to share it immediately, but pausing to check the facts first, once the initial anger fades, often changes how you'd respond to it.

slides.title: Checking a claim in three steps
slides.text: A simple habit for evaluating almost any claim: who said it, what's their evidence, and does anyone independent agree. Running a claim through these three questions catches a surprising number of weak or misleading claims before they take hold.

quiz.question: What does "media literacy" involve?
choices: Understanding who made a piece of media and why
Watching as much media as possible without thinking about it
quiz.explanation: Media literacy means understanding who created a piece of media, why, and who they're trying to persuade, before deciding how much to trust it. An article about a product's benefits written by the company selling it deserves far less automatic trust than an independent review with no financial stake.

quiz.question: A news article summarizes a scientific study. Which one is the primary source?
choices: The original study itself
The news article summarizing it
quiz.explanation: A primary source is the original material itself, like a study or raw data, while a secondary source describes or summarizes it, like a news article about that study. Secondary sources can introduce distortion or spin along the way, even without meaning to.

quiz.question: A 'study' funded by a soda company finds that sugar isn't harmful. What should that funding make you do?
choices: Look at the study with extra scrutiny
Trust it exactly as much as any independent study
quiz.explanation: Checking who funded or profits from a piece of information is a fast way to judge how much scrutiny it deserves. A "study" funded by a soda company that concludes sugar isn't harmful deserves a more skeptical look than an independent study with no financial stake in the result.

quiz.question: What is "propaganda"?
choices: One-sided, emotionally charged messaging meant to persuade
A neutral, balanced news report
quiz.explanation: Propaganda is one-sided, emotionally charged messaging designed to push a viewpoint rather than inform fairly. A message using only scary language and dramatic music to push one opinion, while ignoring all counter-evidence, is a sign you're looking at propaganda rather than balanced information.

quiz.question: Calling a policy a "job-killing disaster" instead of "an economic change" — what's this an example of?
choices: Loaded language chosen to trigger emotion
Neutral, objective description
quiz.explanation: Loaded language uses words picked to trigger an emotional reaction instead of describing something neutrally. Calling a policy a "job-killing disaster" instead of "an economic change" can describe the exact same policy while pushing readers toward a very different feeling about it.

quiz.question: A headline reads "You won't BELIEVE what happened next!" What is this style of headline designed to do?
choices: Provoke a click, often by overstating the actual story
Accurately summarize the story in a neutral way
quiz.explanation: Clickbait headlines, like "you won't BELIEVE what happened next," are engineered to provoke a click rather than accurately summarize the story. They often overstate, distort, or leave out the actual substance of what follows underneath them. In real decisions, the goal is not perfect certainty; it is to update your confidence in proportion to the quality of the evidence.

quiz.question: When researching a controversial topic for a school paper, what produces a more credible paper?
choices: Deliberately reading strong arguments on both sides
Only reading sources that already agree with you
quiz.explanation: Strong critical thinkers weigh the quality and quantity of evidence on all sides before forming a conclusion, instead of just picking whichever side feels comfortable. Deliberately reading strong arguments on both sides of a controversial topic, not just the ones you already agree with, produces a far more credible paper.

quiz.question: Who does the "burden of proof" fall on when someone makes a claim?
choices: The person making the claim
Everyone else, to disprove it
quiz.explanation: The burden of proof means whoever makes a claim is responsible for backing it up with evidence, not the other way around. If someone claims a supplement cures headaches, it's their job to show real evidence for that, not everyone else's job to prove it doesn't.

quiz.question: Why might a strong emotional reaction be worth noticing during a decision?
choices: It might be clouding clear thinking in the moment
Emotions never affect decision-making at all
quiz.explanation: Recognizing when a strong emotion, like anger, excitement, or fear, might be clouding your thinking helps you make clearer decisions under pressure. Feeling furious after an upsetting headline might push you to share it instantly, but pausing to check the facts first often changes how you'd respond.

quiz.question: What's a simple three-step habit for checking a claim?
choices: Who said it, what's their evidence, does anyone independent agree
Believe it once, then never think about it again
quiz.explanation: A simple habit for evaluating almost any claim is asking who said it, what's their evidence, and whether anyone independent agrees. Running a claim through these three questions catches a surprising number of weak or misleading claims before they take hold. In real decisions, the goal is not perfect certainty; it is to update your confidence in proportion to the quality of the evidence.

slides.title: Common logical fallacies
slides.text: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning — like attacking a person instead of their argument, or assuming something is true just because 'everyone believes it.' For example, responding to someone's argument about climate policy by saying "well, you're not even a scientist" attacks the person instead of addressing what they actually said — that's a logical fallacy, not a real rebuttal.

slides.title: The false dilemma
slides.text: A false dilemma presents only two extreme options when more actually exist. "Either you support this exact plan completely, or you don't care about the problem at all" ignores every reasonable middle position between full support and total indifference.

slides.title: The slippery slope
slides.text: A slippery slope argument claims that one small step will inevitably cascade into an extreme outcome, without actually showing why that chain of events would happen. "If we let students retake one quiz, soon nobody will ever study for anything" skips over every reasonable middle possibility in between.

slides.title: Circular reasoning
slides.text: Circular reasoning is an argument that just restates its own conclusion as if that were proof. "This app is the most popular because everyone uses it, and everyone uses it because it's the most popular" goes in a loop without ever landing on any real, independent evidence.

slides.title: Steelmanning an argument
slides.text: Instead of attacking the weakest version of an opposing view, a strong thinker engages with the strongest, most reasonable version of it — called 'steelmanning.' For example, instead of arguing against the silliest version of an opposing political view you've heard, engaging with the most thoughtful argument that side actually makes leads to a much stronger, more honest debate.

slides.title: Building a real argument
slides.text: A solid argument states a clear claim, backs it with real evidence, and directly addresses the strongest objection to it — not just the loudest or weakest voice in the room. Arguments that skip the third step tend to fall apart the moment someone raises a serious counterpoint.

slides.title: Deciding under uncertainty
slides.text: Many real decisions have to be made without knowing everything for certain. Thinking in terms of likely outcomes, not guaranteed ones, leads to better choices. For example, choosing a college major isn't about finding a guaranteed-perfect choice — it's about weighing which path seems most likely to lead somewhere you'd be happy, given what you know now.

slides.title: Expected value, informally
slides.text: A good decision weighs not just whether an outcome would be good or bad, but how likely it actually is. A tiny chance at a huge reward can, depending on the actual numbers, be worth less than a near-certain chance at a merely decent one — it's the combination of size and likelihood that matters, not either alone.

slides.title: The scientific method, briefly
slides.text: Form a question, propose an explanation, test it, and revise based on results — this basic loop underlies careful thinking far beyond just science class. For example, if you wonder "does studying with music help or hurt my focus," you could test it by studying with music some days and without on others, then honestly comparing your results — the same basic loop scientists use.

slides.title: Sample size and small numbers
slides.text: A pattern based on just a few examples — a 'small sample' — can be pure coincidence rather than a real trend, so bigger samples are generally more trustworthy. For example, if three people from a certain town happen to be tall, that says almost nothing about the town in general, but if a study measures three thousand people from that town, the result actually starts to mean something.

It's a strong argument with solid evidence

Ignoring opposing views entirely

quiz.question: What does a solid argument need, beyond just a claim?
choices: Real evidence and a response to the strongest objection
Just being stated loudly and confidently

quiz.question: Why is deciding "under uncertainty" a real skill, like choosing a college major?
choices: Most real decisions don't come with guaranteed outcomes
Every decision in life comes with a guaranteed correct answer
quiz.explanation: Most real decisions, like choosing a college major, don't come with a guaranteed-correct answer known in advance. Thinking in terms of which path seems most likely to lead somewhere good, rather than searching for a certain outcome, leads to better real-world choices.

quiz.question: A tiny chance at a huge reward versus a near-certain chance at a decent reward — what should a good decision weigh?
choices: Both how good the outcome is and how likely it is
Only how good the outcome could be, ignoring likelihood
quiz.explanation: A good decision under uncertainty weighs both how good an outcome would be and how likely it actually is to happen, not just one of those alone. A tiny chance at a huge reward can be worth less than a near-certain chance at a smaller, decent one, depending on the real numbers.

quiz.question: What is the basic loop of the scientific method?
choices: Question, propose an explanation, test it, revise based on results
Guess once and never check again
quiz.explanation: The scientific method's basic loop is: form a question, propose an explanation, test it, and revise based on the results, and this loop underlies careful thinking far beyond science class. Testing whether studying with music helps or hurts your focus, by comparing days with and without it, uses that exact loop.

quiz.question: Three people from a small town happen to be tall. Does that prove the town is full of tall people?
choices: No — a small sample can just be coincidence
Yes, any pattern you notice is automatically true
quiz.explanation: A pattern based on just a few examples, a "small sample," can be pure coincidence rather than a real trend. Three tall people from a town says almost nothing on its own, but measuring three thousand people from that same town starts to actually mean something.
